why.support: Timetables, menus and websites are not for reading every word. Learn where to look. Find answers fast.
why.core: Most of what you read in real life — timetables, menus, websites, forms — isn't meant to be read word by word. If you know where to look, you find the answer in seconds.
why.extend: Websites, timetables and forms are designed for scanning, not reading. Knowing how a text is organised — and how technology has changed the way we read — lets you find, check and compare information in seconds.

articles.title: Read like a detective

body.support:
Need one fact fast? Don't read every word. Use three tricks.

1. **Skim.** Look at the title, headings and pictures. Now you know what it's about.
2. **Scan.** Hunt for one thing, like a time or a price. Let your eyes jump.
3. **Search.** On a website, use the search box. Or press **Ctrl + F** to find a word.

Texts help you. **Headings** tell you what each part is about. **Tables** have rows and columns. Run your finger across and down.

Found it? **Check** it. Right day? Right stop?
body.core:
When you need one fact fast, reading every word is the slow way. Good readers use three tricks.

1. **Skim** to get the main idea. Look at the title, headings, pictures and the first line of each section. In ten seconds you know what the text is about.
2. **Scan** to find one detail. Decide what you're hunting for — a time, a price, a name — and let your eyes jump until you see it. Numbers and bold words stand out.
3. **Search** when the text is long. Use the website's search box, or press **Ctrl + F** (Cmd + F on a Mac) to find a word on the page.

Texts are built to help you. **Headings** tell you what each part is about. **Menus** show a website's main sections. **Tables** put information in rows and columns, so you can run your finger across and down. **Bold** words and **links** jump out.

When you think you've found it, **check**. Is it the right day? The right stop? The right size? A quick check saves a long walk.

caseStudies.title: How little do people read?

body.support:
**Nielsen Norman Group** studies how people use websites.

In 2008, it found most web pages had about **600 words**. But people only read about **20%** of them.

It also found people's eyes often move in an **F shape**. Across the top. Across again. Then down the left side.

So good websites put the important words first.
body.core:
**Nielsen Norman Group** is a company. It studies how people use websites. In 2008 it checked how long people spent on web pages. It also counted the words on each page.

The average page had about **600 words**. But people only had time to read about **28%** of them. The researchers said **20%** was more likely.

The same group also used cameras that track where eyes look. People often read web pages in an **F shape**. They read across the top. Then across a bit lower down. Then down the left side.

So good websites put the most important words first. They use headings, short paragraphs and lists.
body.extend:
**Nielsen Norman Group** is a company that studies how people use websites. In 2008 it compared how long people spent on web pages with how many words those pages had.

The average page had about **600 words**, but people only had time to read about **28%** of them. The researchers estimated **20%** was more realistic, because some time goes on looking at layout and images.

In eye-tracking research, the same group found people often scan web pages in an **F-pattern**: across the top, across a little lower, then down the left side. Designers use this — putting key words first, and using headings, short paragraphs and lists — so the page works for scanners.

teacher.overview: Students learn three navigation strategies — **skim, scan, search** — and how text features (headings, menus, tables, bold) are designed to help readers find information. They apply these to real-world texts (timetables, menus, websites), then reorganise a dense notice so it can be scanned.
prep: Have two real websites ready to model scanning (e.g. a public transport journey planner and a takeaway menu).
Optional: stopwatch for Race the clock.

lessons.title: Lesson 1 — Nobody reads every word
steps: **Hook (5 min):** “The bus leaves in 4 minutes” — show a busy timetable.
**Explicit teaching (15 min):** model skim, scan and search on a real website, thinking aloud.
**Read (15 min):** Read like a detective + Check your reading.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 — Timetables and races
steps: **Case study (15 min):** how little do people read; discuss the F-pattern.

lessons.title: Lesson 3 — Make it scannable
steps: **Model (10 min):** turn a paragraph into a notice with heading and dot points.
**Write (25 min):** final mission; fast finishers Level Up.

teacher.answers:
**Race the clock:** Bus 2 reaches TAFE at 7:50. To reach the Hospital by 8:15, catch Bus 2 (Station 7:35, Hospital 8:01); Bus 3 arrives 8:31 — too late. Bus 3 doesn't stop at the Pool (a dash — see the note).

**Skim, scan or search?** News story — Skim. Chips price — Scan. “Warranty” in a manual — Search. What a site is for — Skim. Shoe size — Scan. Return policy — Search.

**Case study:** about 600 words; people read about 20% (at most 28%). F-pattern = across the top, across lower, down the left.
